summary: The nature, object, and forms of biblical worship; spirit and truth; corporate and private
readingInstruction: Read John 4:19-26, Psalm 95, and Hebrews 12:18-29. Today is a doctrinal pause on worship. Notice who is worshiped, how, and why.
settingTheScene: The Samaritan woman asked Jesus where one should worship, on Mount Gerizim or in Jerusalem. Jesus answered with a statement about worship that changes everything. Psalm 95 is one of the great invitations to worship in the Psalter, and Hebrews 12 describes the nature of worship under the new covenant. Together they teach that worship is the purpose for which we were made, and that it is directed to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit.
observation: “Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father” (John 4:21).
“The hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking such people to worship him” (John 4:23).
“God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24).
“Oh come, let us sing to the LORD; let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation!” (Psalm 95:1).
“Oh come, let us worship and bow down; let us kneel before the LORD, our Maker!” (Psalm 95:6).
“For he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand” (Psalm 95:7).
“Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and thus let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe” (Hebrews 12:28).
“For our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29).
doctrinalFocus: Worship is the response of the whole person to the worth of God. It is what we were made for. In the Bible, true worship has three marks. First, it is directed to the right object: the triune God alone, not any idol, whether carved or imagined. Second, it is offered “in spirit and truth.” Jesus does not abolish outward forms, but he insists that worship be from the heart, by the Spirit, and according to the truth that God has revealed in Christ and in his Word. Third, it is offered through Christ, our mediator. Under the old covenant, worship centered on the temple, the priests, and the sacrifices. Now Jesus is the temple, the priest, and the sacrifice, and we draw near through him. The Reformed tradition has taught that God is to be worshiped as he commands in Scripture, and so gathered worship centers on the reading and preaching of the Word, prayer, singing, and the sacraments. Worship is also all of life: Romans 12:1 calls us to present our bodies as a living sacrifice. It is joyful and reverent at once, for God is both our Father and a consuming fire.
interpretation:
The Samaritan woman raises a question of place. Jesus says the place no longer matters. A new era is beginning in which worship is not tied to a mountain or a building. The reason is that the Father is seeking worshipers, and God is spirit. He cannot be confined to a location. “In spirit” means by the Holy Spirit, who makes the heart alive. “In truth” means according to the reality revealed in Christ, who is the truth.

Psalm 95 gives a picture of what worship looks like. It begins with singing and a joyful noise, because the LORD is a great God and a great King above all gods, who holds the depths of the earth and the heights of the mountains, and made the sea and dry land. Then it moves from joy to reverence: “Let us worship and bow down; let us kneel.” We worship because he is our Maker, and our shepherd, and we are the sheep of his hand. Then the psalm ends with a warning not to harden our hearts as Israel did in the wilderness. Worship requires listening: “Today, if you hear his voice.”

Hebrews 12 contrasts Sinai and Zion. Israel came to a mountain of fire, darkness, and trembling, and begged that no further word be spoken. But believers have come to Mount Zion, to the heavenly Jerusalem, to innumerable angels, to the assembly of the firstborn, to God the judge, and “to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood.” We receive a kingdom that cannot be shaken. Therefore we offer acceptable worship “with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire.”

True worship holds both together: the intimacy of a child with his Father and the awe of a creature before the Holy One.
connection: Deuteronomy 12 and 1 Kings 8 deal with the place of worship under the old covenant. Isaiah 66:1-2 says heaven is God’s throne, and he looks to the humble. Psalm 29:2 says to worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness. Romans 12:1-2 calls for living sacrifice. Philippians 3:3 describes those who worship by the Spirit of God. Revelation 4 and 5 show worship in heaven. Hebrews 10:19-22 invites us to draw near.
application:
Prepare for worship this Sunday: pray, rest well, and arrive ready to listen.

Take one thing you do this week, such as work, and offer it as worship.

Sing Psalm 95 or a hymn to God in private, even if you’re not a singer.
prayerPrompts: Tell God you want to worship in spirit and truth.
Ask him to teach you to worship even when you do not feel like it.
Praise him as the great God and great King.
